title: Harnessing ChatGPT and GPT-4 for evaluating the rheumatology questions of the Spanish access exam to specialized medical training
extended_summary:
This paper examines whether large language models, specifically ChatGPT and GPT-4, can accurately answer rheumatology questions from Spain’s official medical residency entrance exam (MIR) and whether their accompanying clinical reasoning is sound. The broader motivation is to understand whether these tools could be useful in medical education, particularly for exam preparation and learning in rheumatology, while also identifying risks such as misleading but plausible explanations.

The researchers created the RheumaMIR dataset from rheumatology-related MIR exam questions spanning 2009–2010 through 2022–2023. After exclusions, 143 text-based multiple-choice questions were used. Each question was entered into ChatGPT and GPT-4 in Spanish with the added prompt “Justify your answer.” Six rheumatologists independently rated the models’ clinical reasoning on a 1–5 scale, and the study also examined whether performance varied by year, disease category, question type, and patient gender.

The context is specialized medical training in Spain, with the practical target users being medical students or residency applicants preparing for high-stakes exams. This was not a classroom intervention with enrolled learners; rather, it was an evaluation of AI performance on authentic assessment materials used in medical education. The study took place using publicly available exam items and expert evaluations, not with student participants interacting directly with the tools.

The main findings were that GPT-4 substantially outperformed ChatGPT. GPT-4 achieved 93.71% accuracy versus 66.43% for ChatGPT, and it also received slightly higher clinical reasoning scores. The authors conclude that LLMs may be valuable aids for rheumatology education and for creating learning materials, but they warn that confident, plausible-sounding incorrect reasoning may mislead learners. They recommend expert supervision and caution against uncritical use, especially in clinical practice.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI large language model chatbot used for generating natural-language answers and explanations.
identified_tools.use_case: Used to answer 143 Spanish rheumatology multiple-choice questions from the MIR access exam and justify each answer; rheumatologists evaluated answer accuracy and clinical reasoning.

findings.finding_summary: On 143 rheumatology MIR exam questions, ChatGPT answered 95 correctly, for an accuracy of 66.43%. Its performance was significantly lower than GPT-4 (McNemar’s test p-value = 1.17 × 10^-09).
findings.measure: Accuracy on rheumatology MIR multiple-choice exam questions

findings.finding_summary: Six rheumatologists rated ChatGPT’s clinical reasoning on a 1–5 scale. The median (Q1–Q3) average clinical reasoning score was 4.5 (2.33–4.67), and ChatGPT’s reasoning scores were significantly lower than GPT-4 after majority vote (Wilcoxon signed rank test p-value = 4.47 × 10^-09).
findings.measure: Expert-rated clinical reasoning score on 1–5 Likert scale

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI large language model chatbot used for generating natural-language answers and explanations.
identified_tools.use_case: Represents GPT-4 in this paper under the required family normalization; used to answer the same 143 rheumatology MIR questions and provide justifications evaluated by experts.

findings.finding_summary: GPT-4 answered 134 of 143 rheumatology MIR questions correctly, yielding an accuracy of 93.71%. GPT-4 significantly outperformed ChatGPT on exam accuracy (McNemar’s test p-value = 1.17 × 10^-09).
findings.measure: Accuracy on rheumatology MIR multiple-choice exam questions

findings.finding_summary: GPT-4’s clinical reasoning was rated by six rheumatologists on a 1–5 scale, with a median (Q1–Q3) average score of 4.67 (4.5–4.83). Differences in clinical reasoning scores between GPT-4 and ChatGPT were statistically significant after majority vote (Wilcoxon signed rank test p-value = 4.47 × 10^-09).
findings.measure: Expert-rated clinical reasoning score on 1–5 Likert scale

identified_tools.name: Gemini
identified_tools.description: Google large language model family; Bard is normalized to Gemini.
identified_tools.use_case: Bard was included only in supplementary comparison analyses to compare accuracy against ChatGPT/GPT-4 on the same rheumatology exam questions.

findings.finding_summary: In supplementary analyses, Bard achieved 60.84% accuracy on the rheumatology question set. The paper reports this as a comparison point against ChatGPT/GPT-4, without further detailed reasoning analyses in the main results.
findings.measure: Accuracy on rheumatology MIR question set (supplementary comparison)

identified_tools.name: Claude
identified_tools.description: Anthropic large language model family; Claude 2 is normalized to Claude.
identified_tools.use_case: Claude 2 was included only in supplementary comparison analyses to compare accuracy against ChatGPT/GPT-4 on the same rheumatology exam questions.

findings.finding_summary: In supplementary analyses, Claude 2 achieved 79.72% accuracy on the rheumatology question set. The paper presents this as an additional benchmark relative to ChatGPT and GPT-4.
findings.measure: Accuracy on rheumatology MIR question set (supplementary comparison)

quality_tier_rationale: This is an empirical benchmark study of named LLM tools using exam questions and expert ratings, but it is not an RCT or quasi-experimental study of student learning outcomes. The design is observational/performance-evaluation focused.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports strong tool performance on exam-answering and reasoning tasks, especially for GPT-4, but does not measure direct effects on learners or educational attainment. Educational impact is therefore promising but indirect and unclear.
